opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's not going to be one or the other. It's going to be a hybrid, and the interesting engineering question is how we make that hybrid feel seamless.

Right after ChatGPT, most people assumed everything would live in the cloud, and for good reason. The frontier models are huge, and the best capabilities will probably keep showing up there first. If you want the strongest reasoning or a very long context, you'll go to a big data center with lots of GPUs. That's not going away.

But a few things have been happening at the same time. Model compression and quantization have gotten much better. Smaller models trained with better data and distillation have become surprisingly capable. And the hardware we carry around, our laptops and phones, already has a lot of compute: GPUs, NPUs, unified memory. A lot of that compute just sits idle. So the question becomes: why not use it?

That's part of what motivated us to work on projects like MLC-LLM and WebLLM. We wanted to see whether we could take these language models and run them natively on all kinds of devices, even inside a web browser through WebGPU. Once you see a reasonably capable model running locally in your browser, it changes your intuition about what's possible.

There are real reasons to want edge inference. Privacy is a big one. Some data you'd just rather not send out. Latency and offline availability matter for certain applications. And cost matters too. Serving everything from the cloud is expensive, and if part of the workload can be pushed onto devices people already own, the whole ecosystem scales better.

So my view is that we'll see a spectrum. Some tasks will be handled by a small model on your device, some by a mid-sized model nearby, and the hardest ones will get routed to big cloud models, sometimes with agents coordinating across all of them. To make that work, we need good machine learning systems infrastructure: compilers and runtimes that let you deploy the same model across very different hardware without rewriting everything by hand. That's the part I'm most excited about, because it's where ML systems research can really make a difference. The goal is to make AI accessible everywhere, not just in a few places with the biggest clusters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost of cloud serving and shifting some workloads to devices, but does not identify a slowdown in pre-training progress as the reason attention is shifting toward inference cost.

r002.rationale: The response says frontier capabilities will likely appear in the cloud first and describes a cloud-edge spectrum, but does not state that their balance depends on the rate of continued model capability advances.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that it won't be a binary choice. It's going to be a spectrum, and the interesting part is how the two ends start to cooperate.

Right now the cloud is where the frontier lives. The biggest models, the ones that really surprised people after ChatGPT, need a lot of memory and a lot of compute, and the economics of batching many users together on a big GPU cluster are hard to beat. So I don't expect the cloud to go away. If anything, demand for cloud inference grows because more applications get built on top of these models.

But two things are changing quickly. First, models are getting much more efficient per unit of capability. Quantization, better architectures, distillation, speculative decoding, all of that means a model that needed a data center two years ago can run on a laptop or a phone today. Second, the hardware on the edge is improving. Phones have real NPUs now, Apple Silicon has a lot of unified memory, and even consumer GPUs are quite capable. With MLC LLM we've been able to run surprisingly good models directly in a browser through WebGPU, with no server at all. When I first saw that work, it changed my intuition about what's possible locally.

So where does that leave us? I think the natural split is this. Edge will handle the things where latency, privacy, and cost matter most. Personal assistants that know your data, on-device summarization, interactive experiences where you don't want a round trip to a server for every token. Those are a great fit because the model doesn't need to know everything, it needs to know you, and the marginal cost of running it is essentially zero once you have the device.

The cloud will handle the things that need the frontier. Hard reasoning, very long context, tasks where the quality difference of the biggest model actually matters. And I expect a lot of hybrid patterns: a small local model does the first pass or handles the easy ninety percent, and escalates to the cloud only when it needs to. You can think of the local model as a cache, or as a filter, or even as a draft model for speculative decoding across the network.

The thing I care most about, from an infrastructure point of view, is that developers shouldn't have to rewrite their stack to move along that spectrum. The same model should be able to go to a server GPU, a Mac, an Android phone, or a browser, with the compiler doing the heavy lifting of getting good performance on each one. That's really the vision behind TVM and MLC. If deploying to the edge is painful, people default to the cloud by inertia, not because it's the right choice. If it's easy, the balance gets decided by actual tradeoffs, which is how it should be.

So in short: cloud for the frontier, edge for personalization and everyday interaction, and a lot of interesting work in between. I'd bet the edge share grows steadily, more than most people expect, but the cloud stays essential for pushing the ceiling.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see cloud and edge inference coexist. Models like ChatGPT make the cloud very attractive because they require substantial compute, and you can serve a powerful model to many users. But that doesn’t mean every application needs to send everything to the cloud.

On the edge, you have considerations like latency, privacy, and whether you can work without a network connection. As models become more efficient, more tasks can run locally. A system might handle a simpler request on the device and call a larger model in the cloud when it needs more capability.

So I think the interesting question is how to make those pieces work together. There’s a lot of opportunity in the software stack to help developers deploy models across different hardware and choose the right place to run each computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see cloud and edge inference evolve together. With ChatGPT, a lot of the excitement is around very large models, and the cloud is a natural place to run those because they require substantial compute and memory. It also lets you update the model and serve many users efficiently.

But there are strong reasons to bring inference closer to the user: latency, privacy, cost, and the ability to work without a network connection. Not every task needs the largest model. A smaller model running on your phone or laptop could handle many everyday requests, while more difficult requests go to the cloud.

So I think the interesting question is how to make those pieces work together. Can we specialize models for a particular device or task? Can we make deployment efficient across different hardware? The balance will depend on the application, but I expect a spectrum of approaches, with more intelligence both in the cloud and on the device.
